## Where Part 1 left us

- Every method so far tried to **write down** $p_{\text{data}}$ — Gaussian, sparse
  graph, mixture, kernel sum, posterior
- All hit the same wall
- Metropolis–Hastings needs a density it can evaluate. Images do not have one

::: {.note}
So change what the **model is**. Not a formula for a density — a *procedure for
producing a sample*.
:::

## The implicit model

$$z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_k), \qquad x = G_\theta(z) \in \mathbb{R}^d$$

Push low-dimensional noise through a network. The output distribution $p_g$ is a
genuine object — the pushforward $G_\theta \# p_z$.

- You can **draw** from it: one forward pass
- You cannot **evaluate** it: that needs an integral over all $z$ landing at $x$
- Usually it has no density at all — its support is $k$-dimensional inside
  $\mathbb{R}^d$

## Which breaks everything we had

::: {.note}
**Maximum likelihood is unavailable.** Note 06: maximising likelihood *is*
minimising $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}} \| p_\theta)$ — but that requires
evaluating $p_\theta(x_i)$.

**And KL would be useless anyway.** Note 07: two distributions on non-overlapping
manifolds have $\mathrm{KL} = \infty$. That is the generic situation here.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So the loss must be computable from **samples alone** — a batch of real $x$'s and
a batch of fake $G(z)$'s, with no density anywhere.

That single constraint forces everything that follows.
:::

## Police and thief

A **counterfeiter** prints fake notes and wants them to pass.
The **police** inspect notes and want to catch every fake.

- Neither is competent at the start
- Crude fakes teach the police to check the watermark
- Police checking watermarks teach the counterfeiter to print one
- It ends when forgeries are indistinguishable — and the police are reduced to a
  coin flip

::: {.note}
That inability **is** the certificate of success.
:::

## Two details of the analogy *are* the mathematics

**The counterfeiter never sees real money.**
$G$ has no access to the training set. Not one gradient in the generator's update
touches a real image. Everything it learns arrives *through* $D$.

::: {.fragment}
**The police hand over their reasoning, not just their verdict.**
$D$ is differentiable, so $G$ receives $\nabla_x D(x)$ — the *direction in image
space* that would make the note more convincing.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Rejection sampling throws away a rejected dart and learns nothing. A GAN turns
every rejection into a **direction**.
:::

## The objective

$D_\phi(x) \in (0,1)$ is the probability that $x$ is real — a binary classifier
trained with cross-entropy on real vs. generated:

$$V(D,G) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big]
\;+\; \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(z))\big)\big]$$

$D$ wants this **large**; $G$ wants the second term **small**. One quantity, two
opposed interests:

$$\boxed{\;\min_G \max_D \; V(D,G)\;}$$

## The order matters

$$\min_G \;\underbrace{\max_D \; V(D,G)}_{\text{inner}}$$

The generator is judged against the **best available** critic, not a fixed one.

::: {.note}
Otherwise $G$ finds the one blind spot of a mediocre $D$ and parks there. Hold on
to this — when alternating optimisation drifts toward the *other* order, we get
mode collapse.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Note also: $\mathbb{E}_{z}[\log(1-D(G(z)))] = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g}[\log(1-D(x))]$.
The latent has disappeared; only two distributions remain.
:::

## Step 1 — the optimal discriminator

Write both expectations over the same variable:

$$V(D,G) \;=\; \int \Big[\,p_{\text{data}}(x)\log D(x) + p_g(x)\log\big(1-D(x)\big)\Big] dx$$

::: {.fragment}
$D(x)$ at one point appears in the integrand **only** at that point. So — allowing
$D$ to be any function — maximise the bracket **pointwise**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
With $a = p_{\text{data}}(x)$, $b = p_g(x)$, $t = D(x)$:

$$f(t) = a\log t + b\log(1-t), \qquad f'(t) = \frac{a}{t} - \frac{b}{1-t}$$
:::

## Step 1 — solve it

$$\frac{a}{t} = \frac{b}{1-t} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t^{*} = \frac{a}{a+b},
\qquad f''(t) = -\frac{a}{t^2} - \frac{b}{(1-t)^2} < 0$$

::: {.fragment}
$$\boxed{\;D^{*}_G(x) \;=\; \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_{\text{data}}(x) + p_g(x)}\;}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
At the solution $p_g = p_{\text{data}}$, this is $\tfrac12$ **everywhere** — the
coin flip, exactly as the story promised.
:::

## The discriminator is a density-ratio estimator

With $r = p_{\text{data}}/p_g$:

$$D^{*} = \frac{r}{1+r}, \qquad r(x) = \frac{D^{*}(x)}{1 - D^{*}(x)}$$

Write $D = \sigma(h)$ for a logit $h$. Then

$$\boxed{\;h^{*}(x) \;=\; \log \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_g(x)}\;}$$

::: {.note}
Two densities nobody can write down — and a **classifier recovers their ratio from
samples alone**. This is the single most reusable idea in the lecture.
:::

## Step 2 — what is $G$ actually minimising?

Define the mixture — the *average of the data and generated distributions*:

$$m \;=\; \tfrac12\big(p_{\text{data}} + p_g\big),
\qquad D^{*} = \frac{p_{\text{data}}}{2m}, \qquad 1 - D^{*} = \frac{p_g}{2m}$$

::: {.fragment}
Substitute into $V$:

$$C(G) = \mathbb{E}_{p_{\text{data}}}\!\left[\log \frac{p_{\text{data}}}{2m}\right]
+ \mathbb{E}_{p_g}\!\left[\log \frac{p_g}{2m}\right]$$
:::

## Step 2 — pull out the twos

$$C(G) = \mathbb{E}_{p_{\text{data}}}\!\left[\log \frac{p_{\text{data}}}{m}\right] - \log 2
+ \mathbb{E}_{p_g}\!\left[\log \frac{p_g}{m}\right] - \log 2$$

[each $\log(2m)$ splits as $\log 2 + \log m$]{.step}

::: {.fragment}
$$C(G) = -\log 4 \;+\; \mathrm{KL}\big(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, m\big)
+ \mathrm{KL}\big(p_g \,\|\, m\big)$$

[each expectation of a log-ratio is a KL, by definition]{.step}
:::

::: {.fragment}
And those two KLs against the mixture are, by definition, twice the
**Jensen–Shannon** divergence.
:::

## The theorem

$$\boxed{\;C(G) \;=\; -\log 4 \;+\; 2\,\mathrm{JS}\big(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, p_g\big)\;}$$

::: {.note}
**Goodfellow et al. (2014).** $\mathrm{JS} \ge 0$ with equality only when the two
distributions coincide. So the global minimum of $C(G)$ is attained **exactly** at
$p_g = p_{\text{data}}$, with value $-\log 4 \approx -1.386$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A construction motivated by a story about counterfeiters turns out to minimise a
specific, symmetric, principled divergence.

**The adversary was never a heuristic — it is a variational estimator of a
divergence**, computing by optimisation what has no closed form.
:::

## Read the small print

Three gaps between the theorem and anything you can run:

1. **$D$ is not optimal.** $D^{*}$ assumed an unconstrained function and exact
   maximisation. In practice: a network, a few steps per generator update
2. **$G$ moves in parameter space.** The convexity argument treats $p_g$ itself as
   the variable. In $\theta$, $C$ is not convex — the proof does not transfer, and
   the paper says so
3. **Minibatch gradients**, in a game where the two players' noise is coupled

::: {.note}
Every difficulty that follows comes through one of these three gaps.
:::

## Training, as implemented

**$k$ discriminator steps** (usually $k=1$) — ascend

$$\frac1m \sum_{i=1}^{m}\Big[\log D_\phi(x_i) + \log\big(1 - D_\phi(G_\theta(z_i))\big)\Big]$$

**One generator step** — descend its loss on fresh latents.

::: {.note}
$D$ chases a **moving target**: every generator step changes $p_g$, and therefore
changes $D^{*}$. Chasing too closely turns out to be as bad as not chasing at all.
:::

## Difficulty 1 — the generator's gradient vanishes

The min-max objective gives $G$ the loss $\mathbb{E}_z\big[\log(1 - D(G(z)))\big]$.
Write $D = \sigma(h)$:

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial h}\,\log\big(1 - \sigma(h)\big) \;=\; -\,\sigma(h) \;=\; -D$$

::: {.fragment}
Early in training $G$'s samples are obvious fakes, so $D(G(z)) \approx 0$ — and the
gradient reaching $G$ is **proportional to $D(G(z))$**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {style="text-align:center"}
[The generator learns most slowly exactly when it is worst.]{.big}
:::
:::

## The non-saturating fix

Have $G$ **maximise $\log D(G(z))$** instead of minimising $\log(1-D(G(z)))$. Same
fixed point — both want $D(G(z)) \to 1$ — but

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial h}\big(-\log \sigma(h)\big) \;=\; -\big(1 - \sigma(h)\big) \;=\; -(1-D)
\;\longrightarrow\; -1 \ \text{ as } D \to 0$$

::: {.note}
Now the gradient is **largest** when the samples are worst. Essentially every GAN
ever trained uses this.
:::

## What the fix costs

Arjovsky & Bottou (2017): at an optimal discriminator, the non-saturating
generator gradient is the gradient of

$$\mathrm{KL}\big(p_g \,\|\, p_{\text{data}}\big) \;-\; 2\,\mathrm{JS}\big(p_g \,\|\, p_{\text{data}}\big)$$

- **Reverse** KL — note 07: *mode-seeking*. Punishes mass where there is none;
  nearly indifferent to missing an entire mode
- The JS term enters with a **minus sign** — actively pushing $p_g$ *away*

::: {.note}
The loss people actually train is not a divergence, is mode-seeking, and contains
a repulsive term. Mode collapse is visible in the objective.
:::

## Difficulty 1, the deeper version

Note 07 §8: if $p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_g$ have essentially **disjoint supports** —
generic, since both are manifolds in a high-dimensional space —

$$\mathrm{JS}(p_{\text{data}} \| p_g) = \log 2 \quad\text{exactly},
\qquad \nabla_\theta\,\mathrm{JS} = 0$$

Not small. **Zero.** "Maximally different", with no direction attached.

::: {.note}
::: {style="text-align:center"}
[The theory wants $D$ optimal. An optimal $D$ gives no gradient.]{.big}
:::
:::

## That dilemma, and the way out

- A **near-perfect** $D$ separates the manifolds cleanly, is confident everywhere,
  and is therefore flat everywhere $G$ can reach
- A **weak** $D$ gives a usable gradient pointing in the wrong direction
- Training lives in the narrow band between, held there by hand-tuned learning
  rates, architectures and update ratios

::: {.note}
The non-saturating loss patches the symptom. **WGAN removes the cause**: replace JS
with $W_1$, which reports the actual distance between separated supports and keeps
a gradient pointing home. That is why note 07 came before this lecture.
:::

## Difficulty 2 — mode collapse

$G$ maps every latent to the same output, or a handful. Ten digit classes in,
convincing sevens out — and nothing else. Three explanations, all correct:

::: {.fragment}
**The min and max swap.** Alternating optimisation drifts toward $\max_D \min_G$.
There, $G$ moves first against a *fixed* $D$, and its optimal response is to put
all mass on $\arg\max_x D(x)$ — a **delta function** is the exact solution.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**The divergence is mode-seeking** — reverse KL covers one mode well rather than
all modes poorly.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Nothing penalises missing mass.** $D$ judges samples **one at a time**. Diversity
is a property of a *set*, invisible to a pointwise classifier.
:::

## The same pathology as Part 1

::: {.note}
An MH chain trapped in one mode looks perfectly healthy — good acceptance, stable
trace — while sampling the wrong distribution.

A mode-collapsed GAN looks perfectly healthy — sharp samples, low losses — while
modelling the wrong distribution.
:::

::: {style="text-align:center"}
[Locally correct everywhere; globally wrong. And in both cases the diagnostic that
would reveal it is the one the algorithm never computes.]{.big}
:::

## Difficulty 3 — it is a game, not a minimisation

Ordinary training minimises **one** function, and "the loss went down" means
progress. Here the target is a **saddle point**, and descending a loss is not a
correct algorithm for finding one.

::: {.fragment}
The smallest instance: $\min_x \max_y \; xy$, equilibrium at the origin.
Simultaneous gradient steps of size $\eta$:

$$x_{t+1} = x_t - \eta\,y_t, \qquad y_{t+1} = y_t + \eta\,x_t$$
:::

## The iterates spiral outward

$$x_{t+1}^2 + y_{t+1}^2 = (x_t - \eta y_t)^2 + (y_t + \eta x_t)^2
= (1+\eta^2)\big(x_t^2 + y_t^2\big)$$

[the cross terms cancel exactly]{.step}

::: {.fragment}
Distance from the equilibrium **grows at every step**, for any $\eta > 0$. As
$\eta \to 0$ the iterates orbit forever and never converge.
:::

::: {.note}
This is a convex–concave game — the friendliest case that exists — and gradient
descent-ascent still fails on it.
:::

## What that means in the room

- **The losses tell you nothing.** $D$'s loss near $\log 2$ is what you want, and
  also what you see when everything has collapsed. No scalar's descent means
  progress — evaluation moves outside the training loop entirely (FID, Inception
  Score, human inspection)
- **Oscillation.** Sample quality visibly cycles: sharp, degraded, sharp. You
  checkpoint often and pick by eye
- **Balance is a hyperparameter.** $D$ too strong → no gradient. $G$ too strong →
  collapse. Two learning rates, two architectures, one update ratio, tuned jointly

## Difficulty 4 — slow, and expensive

- **Two coupled networks.** $D$ must be near-optimal *for the current $p_g$* — which
  just changed. Much of the compute goes into tracking, not progress
- **Indirect signal.** $G$ never touches a real sample; everything arrives
  second-hand through $D$
- **No likelihood, so no model selection.** No held-out log-likelihood, no early
  stopping, no overfitting detection. A memorising GAN and a generalising one
  produce equally pretty samples
- **Sensitivity.** That an entire paper (DCGAN) was needed to publish *a set of
  architectural choices that trains reliably* is the evidence

## What was done about it

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Vanishing gradient | non-saturating loss |
| Vanishing gradient | **WGAN** + gradient penalty — swap JS for $W_1$, an IPM |
| Vanishing gradient | instance noise — make the supports overlap |
| Mode collapse | minibatch discrimination — let $D$ see batch statistics |
| Mode collapse | unrolled GANs — let $G$ see $D$'s future response |
| Instability | spectral normalisation; two time-scale updates |
| Generality | **$f$-GAN** — the same template for any $f$-divergence |

## Instance noise is diffusion in embryo

The fix for disjoint supports: **add Gaussian noise to both real and fake
samples**, so both acquire full support and the ratio becomes finite again.

It works. It was regarded as a trick.

::: {.note}
A diffusion model does this at **every noise level, simultaneously and
deliberately**. The forward process is a whole continuum of noised versions of
$p_{\text{data}}$, and the model learns to reverse each level.

What GANs had to smuggle in as a stabiliser is the diffusion model's organising
principle.
:::

## The two halves of today are one machine

| | Metropolis–Hastings | GAN |
|---|---|---|
| Proposal | chosen by hand | **learned** |
| Density ratio | computed from $\tilde\pi$ | **estimated** by a classifier |
| Requires | $\tilde\pi(x)$ evaluable | samples only |
| A rejection | chain stays put | becomes a **direction** |
| Output | exact, correlated draws | approximate, independent draws |
| Per sample | thousands of steps, every time | one forward pass |

::: {.note}
A trained $D$ gives a density ratio for two distributions nobody can write down —
so you can run an MH accept/reject step on a GAN's own samples. That is exactly
what MH-GAN (2019) does.
:::

## Three sentences to leave with

**The construction.** No likelihood means the loss must come from samples;
a classifier separating real from fake supplies it, and its logit is the log
density ratio.

**The theorem.** At an optimal $D$ the game minimises
$-\log 4 + 2\,\mathrm{JS}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_g)$, uniquely minimised at
$p_g = p_{\text{data}}$.

**The trouble.** JS saturates between disjoint manifolds, killing the gradient
exactly when $D$ is good; and a saddle point is not a minimum, so descent has no
reason to converge.

## Where this leaves the course

A GAN is a **learned proposal with a learned judge**. It fixed what was wrong with
Metropolis–Hastings — and inherited a new problem: the judge is an adversary.

::: {.note}
The rest of this course **removes the judge**. A diffusion model's forward process
adds a *small* amount of noise at each of many steps, so each reverse step is
nearly Gaussian and can be matched by direct regression against a target computed
from real data.

No adversary. No saddle point. No accept/reject. And a loss whose descent means
progress.
:::

::: {.quote}
You cannot write the density down, so you train a critic to smell the difference —
and it turns out you were minimising Jensen–Shannon all along.
